lesson.title: Fencing the Yard: Solving Perimeter Word Problems
lesson.summary: Use the perimeter formulas for rectangles and other polygons together with the applications of linear equations strategy to find unknown side lengths from a total perimeter.
lesson.body:
Perimeter problems take a geometric fact you likely already know, that the perimeter of a shape is the total distance around its outside edge, and combine it with the equation building skills from applications of linear equations. For a rectangle with length l and width w, the perimeter formula is P equals 2l plus 2w, since a rectangle has two sides of each length. For a triangle, the perimeter is simply the sum of its three side lengths, a plus b plus c. What makes these into algebra problems, rather than plain geometry, is that one or more of the side lengths is described only in words, in relation to another side, and has to be represented with a variable before the formula can be used.

The setup step is almost always the hardest part. A phrase like "the length is 5 feet more than twice the width" needs to be translated the same way any other word problem phrase is translated: if w represents the width, then twice the width is 2w, and 5 more than that is 2w plus 5, so the length is 2w plus 5. Once every side is written in terms of a single variable, that expression is substituted into the appropriate perimeter formula, and the resulting equation is solved using the same balancing steps used throughout this unit.

Here is a full example. The length of a rectangular garden is 5 feet more than twice its width, and the perimeter of the garden is 46 feet. Find the dimensions. Let w equal the width, in feet. Then the length is 2w plus 5, following the translation above. The perimeter formula for a rectangle is 2l plus 2w equals P, so substituting gives 2 times the quantity 2w plus 5, plus 2w, equals 46. Distributing the 2 gives 4w plus 10 plus 2w equals 46. Combining the like terms 4w and 2w gives 6w plus 10 equals 46. Subtracting 10 from both sides gives 6w equals 36, and dividing both sides by 6 gives w equals 6. The width is 6 feet, so the length is 2 times 6 plus 5, which is 17 feet.

Checking the answer means plugging both dimensions back into the perimeter formula rather than just verifying the last equation balanced. Two times the length, 17, is 34, and two times the width, 6, is 12, and 34 plus 12 equals 46, which matches the perimeter given in the problem. It is also worth checking the original relationship in words: is 17 really 5 more than twice 6? Twice 6 is 12, and 5 more than 12 is 17, so yes, both conditions are satisfied.

Perimeter problems appear with other shapes too, such as isosceles triangles where two sides are described as equal and a third side is described in terms of the first, or figures where the perimeter itself is unknown and a side length is given instead. In every case the strategy is the same: represent every unknown side using one variable, substitute into the correct perimeter formula for the shape, solve, and check both the perimeter total and the verbal relationship between the sides.
